text.p: After more than 30 years in the "little bit of country and a little bit of rock and roll" business, Marie Osmond has moved on from child star to mother of five, theatre performer and savvy business woman.
But she still exudes the wholesome goodness that was her trademark when she entered show business.

"I have lived an amazing life...worked with just about everybody you can imagine, but there are not a lot of people who've bridged the gap between child star and adult," Osmond said in an interview with Reuters.

On tour to promote her performance as Maria in "The Sound of Music", to be staged this year in Singapore, Thailand and Hong Kong, Osmond is planning to publish her autobiography in a couple of years' time.

Over 30 years ago, Andy Williams hoisted up a pint-sized, dark haired toddler on to his lap in front of his weekly television show's millions of viewers and introduced her as "the youngest Osmond Brother".
The only daughter in the famous musical Mormon family from Utah did not follow six of her brothers into pop and rock.
Instead she made country music history at 13 by hitting the number one chart position with a debut record, "Paper Roses".
At 14, she became the youngest person to co-host a weekly television variety series when she joined her brother on "The Donny and Marie Show".
After gaining a world-wide audience with the show's five-year run, Osmond headed for the quieter pastures of country music's Mecca, Nashville, to record hit country songs.

"I never was a normal child... I never went to public school. I worked 16 to 18-hour days, six days a week. I never did anything normal," she said. "I couldn't date till I was 16 and when I turned 16, nobody had my phone number."
NO BED OF PAPER ROSES
But that did not stop her from marrying childhood sweetheart and basketball star Steve Craig in 1982, a rocky relationship that ended in divorce three years later.
"There were just a lot of things about my life that were difficult... I went through a difficult first marriage, I know what it's like to be a single parent," she said.
Having grown up in a family of nine children that still congregates at least once a year, Osmond married again in 1986, this time to music producer and composer Brian Blosil.
Osmond is now the mother of five children, whose ages range from four months to 14 years. She said she would encourage her children to follow in her show business tracks if they want to.

She described proudly how her eldest son, Stephen, her only child from her first marriage, successfully auditioned for a role in the U.S. tour of "The Sound of Music" without anyone knowing he was her son.

"I feel very fortunate that I have been able to travel with them (her children), continue working and growing myself," she said. "My husband is supportive...we really have a wonderful life, we have been very blessed. God has been good to me."
She said her children were the inspiration for her autobiography.

"I just started doing it really for my children so they know their mother's life," said Osmond. "I will be very honest. I want it to be truthful because I want my children to know my life has not been easy."
GLASS HALF FULL, NOT HALF EMPTY
"My whole life has been hard, but I choose to be the kind of person that likes to see the glass half full, rather than half empty," she said.
"There a lot of reasons why I think I was able to make that transition...my family background, my strong work ethic that I've developed, my beliefs of God."
Five years ago, Osmond discovered a love for sculpting porcelain doll figures, turning her passion into an award winning, $70 million collector doll business.

Before showing off her dolls for the cameras, one modelled on her mother as a baby and one of herself -- Baby Marie -- with her trademark beauty spot just by her right eye, Osmond quickly adjusts and preens the doll's hair.
"I am silly...but I have fun," she giggles.

On a more serious side, Osmond is fiercely proud of co-founding the Children's Miracle Network, one of the largest fund raising charities in the world, raising well over $1 billion since 1983 for free health care for children.
So can fans expect Osmond to reveal deep dark secrets in her autobiography?
"No, I am who I am,' she said, flashing her trademark grin.
